results.title: A subgroup stabilizing a subset has order dividing its size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ and let $U$ be a subset of $G$ such that $hu \in U$ for all $h \in H$ and $u \in U$. Then $|H|$ divides $|U|$.

results.title: Burnside's lemma with a uniform fixed-point count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let a finite group $G$ act on a finite set $X$, and let $c$ be a natural number such that every element $g \ne 1$ of $G$ fixes exactly $c$ points of $X$. Writing $N$ for the number of orbits of $G$ on $X$, we have $|X| + c\,(|G| - 1) = N \cdot |G|$.

results.title: Frobenius's theorem on the Frobenius kernel
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let a finite group $G$ act faithfully and transitively on a finite set $X$ with at least two elements, such that every point stabiliser is nontrivial and no nonidentity element of $G$ fixes two distinct points of $X$. Then the set consisting of the identity together with the elements of $G$ that fix no point of $X$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.

results.title: Orders of finite $5$-transitive permutation groups
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let a finite group $G$ act faithfully on a finite set $X$ with $n = |X| \ge 5$, and suppose that the action is $5$-transitive: for any two injective maps $a, b \colon \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\} \to X$ there is $g \in G$ with $g \cdot a(i) = b(i)$ for all $i$. Then $|G| = n!$, or $n \ge 7$ and $|G| = n!/2$, or $n = 12$ and $|G| = 95040$, or $n = 24$ and $|G| = 244823040$.

results.title: The conductor-aspect Dirichlet subconvexity exponent
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The infimum, taken in the extended real numbers, of the set of all real $\theta$ that are admissible conductor-aspect exponents for primitive Dirichlet characters. If no real number is admissible, this infimum is $+\infty$.

results.title: The Dirichlet subconvexity exponent is nonnegative
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The conductor-aspect Dirichlet subconvexity exponent, an extended real number, is at least $0$. This holds by construction: every admissible exponent is nonnegative, and if no real exponent is admissible, the exponent is the infimum of the empty set, which is $+\infty$.

results.title: Admissible exponents bound the Dirichlet subconvexity exponent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a real number $\theta$ is an admissible conductor-aspect exponent for primitive Dirichlet characters, then the conductor-aspect Dirichlet subconvexity exponent is at most $\theta$, as extended real numbers.

results.title: Burgess's bound for Dirichlet central values

results.summary: The number $3/16$ is an admissible conductor-aspect exponent for primitive Dirichlet characters: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are a real number $C > 0$ and a natural number $Q$ such that for every positive integer $q \ge Q$ and every primitive Dirichlet character $\chi$ modulo $q$, the analytically continued Dirichlet $L$-function satisfies $|L(1/2, \chi)| \le C q^{3/16 + \varepsilon}$.

results.title: Blumberg's theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ there is a dense set $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that the restriction of $f$ to $D$ is continuous.

results.title: Continuous midpoint-convex functions are convex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a < b$ be real numbers and let $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $(a, b)$ and satisfy $\varphi\bigl(\frac{x+y}{2}\bigr) \le \frac{\varphi(x) + \varphi(y)}{2}$ for all $x, y \in (a, b)$. Then $\varphi$ is convex on $(a, b)$.

results.title: Discontinuous subadditive multiplicative functions on $\mathbb{C}$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a function $\varphi : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{R}$ that is not continuous, satisfies $\varphi(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{C}$, is not identically $0$ and not identically $1$, and satisfies $\varphi(x + y) \le \varphi(x) + \varphi(y)$ and $\varphi(xy) = \varphi(x)\varphi(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{C}$.

results.title: Isolated points of a graph are countable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $F$ be the set of $x\in E$ for which there is a sequence $(x_k)$ in $E\setminus\{x\}$ with $x_k \to x$ and $f(x_k) \to f(x)$. Then $E \setminus F$ is countable.

results.title: Steinhaus's periodization problem (Scottish Book Problem 181)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a continuous function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(x) > 0$ for every real $x$ such that, for every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} f(x + n)$ converges and its sum is $1$.

part.title: Fibonacci word
api: Finite Fibonacci words agree with the infinite Fibonacci word

results.title: Fibonacci substitution
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Fibonacci substitution sends each letter of the binary alphabet $\{0, 1\}$ to a finite binary word: it maps $0$ to $01$ and $1$ to $0$.

results.title: Fibonacci morphism
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Fibonacci morphism $\varphi$ extends the Fibonacci substitution $\sigma$, which maps $0$ to $01$ and $1$ to $0$, to finite binary words by concatenation: $\varphi$ maps the empty word to the empty word, and $\varphi(bw) = \sigma(b)\varphi(w)$ for every letter $b$ and every finite binary word $w$.

results.title: Finite Fibonacci words
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The finite Fibonacci words $f_n$, for natural numbers $n$, are the words in the letters $0$ and $1$ defined by $f_0 = 0$ and $f_{n+1} = \varphi(f_n)$, where $\varphi$ is the Fibonacci morphism, which replaces each letter $0$ by $01$ and each letter $1$ by $0$.

results.title: Infinite Fibonacci word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$), so that $f_0, f_1, f_2, \ldots$ are the finite Fibonacci words $0, 01, 010, 01001, \ldots$. The one-sided infinite Fibonacci word is the infinite binary word whose letter at index $n$ (indices start at $0$) is the letter of $f_{n+2}$ at index $n$.

results.title: The Fibonacci morphism respects concatenation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\varphi$ be the Fibonacci morphism on finite binary words, induced by $0 \mapsto 01$ and $1 \mapsto 0$. For all finite binary words $a$ and $b$, $\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$, where juxtaposition denotes concatenation.

results.title: The Fibonacci morphism does not shorten words
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\varphi$ be the Fibonacci morphism on finite binary words, induced by $0 \mapsto 01$ and $1 \mapsto 0$. For every finite binary word $w$, the length of $\varphi(w)$ is at least the length of $w$, that is, $|w| \le |\varphi(w)|$.

results.title: Finite Fibonacci words begin with $0$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For every natural number $n$, there is a finite binary word $t$ such that $f_n = 0t$, that is, the first letter of $f_n$ is $0$.

results.title: Lower bound on the length of the finite Fibonacci words
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For every natural number $n$, the word $f_n$ has length at least $n + 1$.

results.title: Consecutive finite Fibonacci words are nested
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the $n$-th finite Fibonacci word $f_n$ is a prefix of $f_{n+1}$: there is a finite word $t$ in the letters $0$ and $1$ with $f_{n+1} = f_n t$.

results.title: Earlier finite Fibonacci words are prefixes of later ones
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n \le m$, the $n$-th finite Fibonacci word $f_n$ is a prefix of the $m$-th finite Fibonacci word $f_m$: there is a finite word $t$ in the letters $0$ and $1$ with $f_m = f_n t$.

results.title: Appending a word does not change earlier letters
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ and $t$ be finite words in the letters $0$ and $1$, and let $k$ be a natural number smaller than the length of $a$. Then the letter at position $k$ of the concatenation $a t$ equals the letter at position $k$ of $a$, counting positions from $0$.

results.title: Letters of the finite Fibonacci words stabilize
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For all natural numbers $n \le m$ and every index $i$ less than the length of $f_n$ (indices start at $0$), the letter of $f_m$ at index $i$ equals the letter of $f_n$ at index $i$.

results.title: The finite Fibonacci word of index $n + 2$ has more than $n$ letters
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For every natural number $n$, the length of $f_{n+2}$ is greater than $n$.

results.title: Finite Fibonacci words agree with the infinite Fibonacci word
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For all natural numbers $m$ and $n$ such that $n$ is less than the length of $f_m$, the letter of $f_m$ at index $n$ equals the letter at index $n$ of the one-sided infinite Fibonacci word (indices start at $0$). In other words, every $f_m$ is a prefix of the infinite Fibonacci word.

results.title: Recurrence for the finite Fibonacci words
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f_0, f_1, f_2, \ldots$ be the finite Fibonacci words. For every natural number $n$, $f_{n+2} = f_{n+1} f_n$, where juxtaposition denotes concatenation.

results.title: Concatenating the finite Fibonacci words
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $N$, prepending the letters $0$ and $1$ to the concatenation $f_0 f_1 \cdots f_{N-1}$ of the first $N$ finite Fibonacci words gives $f_{N+1}$: that is, $0\,1\,f_0 f_1 \cdots f_{N-1} = f_{N+1}$, where the concatenation is empty when $N = 0$.

results.title: Finite Fibonacci words are prefixes of the infinite Fibonacci word
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the finite Fibonacci word $f_n$ is the word formed by the first $|f_n|$ letters of the infinite Fibonacci word.

results.title: Factorization of the infinite Fibonacci word into finite Fibonacci words
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be the infinite Fibonacci word and let $f_0, f_1, f_2, \ldots$ be the finite Fibonacci words. For every natural number $N$, the finite word $w_N = 0\,1\,f_0 f_1 \cdots f_{N-1}$ (so $w_0 = 01$) consists of the first $|w_N|$ letters of $f$, and for every natural number $k$ the first $k$ letters of $f$ form a prefix of $w_N$ for some $N$. In this sense $f = 0 \cdot 1 \cdot f_0 \cdot f_1 \cdot f_2 \cdots$.

results.title: Boolean gates
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The Boolean gates are a NOT gate and, for each natural number $a$, an AND gate and an OR gate indexed by $a$, which stand for gates with $a + 1$ inputs. The numbers of inputs are assigned by the Boolean signature, so there is no AND or OR gate with zero inputs.

results.title: Boolean signature
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Boolean signature has the Boolean gates as its operation symbols, where NOT has arity $1$ and, for each natural number $a$, the AND gate and the OR gate indexed by $a$ have arity $a + 1$. In particular, no AND or OR gate takes zero inputs.

results.title: Boolean interpretation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Boolean interpretation evaluates the gates of the Boolean signature on the truth values $\{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$: NOT sends its input $x$ to $\lnot x$, and for each natural number $a$, the AND gate and the OR gate with inputs $x_0, \dots, x_a$ return $(\cdots((\mathrm{true} \land x_0) \land x_1) \cdots) \land x_a$ and $(\cdots((\mathrm{false} \lor x_0) \lor x_1) \cdots) \lor x_a$ respectively, that…

results.title: Boolean NOT
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Under the Boolean interpretation, the NOT gate applied to a truth value $x$ returns its negation $\lnot x$.

results.title: Boolean AND as a left fold
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $a$ and truth values $x_0, \dots, x_a$, the Boolean interpretation of the AND gate with $a + 1$ inputs, applied to $x_0, \dots, x_a$, returns $(\cdots((\mathrm{true} \land x_0) \land x_1) \cdots) \land x_a$, folding conjunction over the inputs from left to right starting from true.

results.title: Boolean OR as a left fold
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $a$ and truth values $x_0, \dots, x_a$, the Boolean interpretation of the OR gate with $a + 1$ inputs, applied to $x_0, \dots, x_a$, returns $(\cdots((\mathrm{false} \lor x_0) \lor x_1) \cdots) \lor x_a$, folding disjunction over the inputs from left to right starting from false.

results.title: Mean fitness stays positive under diploid selection
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Mean fitness stays positive after one generation of diploid viability selection (for nonnegative frequencies and fitnesses; normalization is not needed).

results.title: Diploid Baum–Eagon mean-fitness inequality, sharp form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With nonnegative allele frequencies and genotype fitnesses and positive mean fitness, one generation of selection raises the log mean fitness by at least twice the relative entropy `∑ i, p'_i log (p'_i / p_i)` of the new allele frequencies `p'` from the old ones `p` (Baum–Eagon's argument for the quadratic form `w̄`). Alleles absent before selection stay absent (`p_i = 0 → p'_i = 0`), so the summands with `p_i = 0`…

results.title: Mean fitness never decreases
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Mean fitness never decreases under diploid multi-allele viability selection with random mating (Mulholland–Smith 1959; Scheuer–Mandel 1959; Kingman 1961).

results.title: Mean fitness is unchanged exactly at selection equilibria
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Mean fitness is unchanged by one generation of selection exactly when the allele frequencies are at an equilibrium of the selection map.

results.title: Diploid selection strictly increases mean fitness off equilibria
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Away from equilibria, mean fitness strictly increases under diploid viability selection.

results.title: Derivative of two-allele mean fitness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For two alleles with frequencies `(x, 1 - x)`, the mean fitness `w̄(x) = x² w₀₀ + x (1 - x) (w₀₁ + w₁₀) + (1 - x)² w₁₁` has derivative `2 (m₀ - m₁)`, twice the difference of the marginal fitnesses. This holds for every real `x`.

results.title: Wright's formula
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Wright's formula (Wright 1937): for two alleles with frequencies `(x, 1 - x)`, one generation of viability selection changes the frequency of allele `0` by `Δx = x (1 - x) (dw̄/dx) / (2 w̄)`. The identity is algebraic and holds for every real `x` with `w̄(x) ≠ 0`; the model domain is `x ∈ [0, 1]` with nonnegative fitnesses.
